title: stewardship learning log - production notes and paper skims
content:
Context: personal scratchpad for translating recent paper skims and a few conference talks into practical checks and small experiments I can run on the dev cluster. Audience: me, but will share with devex and serving-runtime folks if any of these actions look promising.

High-level goal: build a short list of high-leverage, low-effort probes that tell us how candidate model changes (quant, kernel selection, routing) affect tail latency, token cost, and hallucination risk in the Redwood hosted flow.

Quick synthesis of recent reads (very brief):
- "Local KV compaction for long context" (paper skim): idea is to compress older KV entries using an autoencoder-like projection so the live KV remains small. Tradeoffs: decoder cost on cache fill, potential degradation for exact recall. Practical thought: try an -offline- compaction experiment where we compress beyond N tokens and replay a small evaluation set to measure hit-rate vs quality.
- "Adaptive batching with latency-SLA aware priority" (talk): keep a small fast-path queue for SLA-critical requests and a separate batcher for best-effort. Implementation thought: experiment with two weight classes in our current batching proxy (fast 0-10 ms; slow 50-200 ms). Measure cost delta when diverting 10% of traffic to fast-path.
- "Quantization-aware prompt rewriting" (blog): rewrite prompts to be quantization-friendly (less token churn, avoid ambiguous punctuation) to reduce model sensitivity after int8/4bit. Small test: pick a few representative prompts and run with fp16 vs int4 model variants and compute BLEU/ROUGE and spot-check hallucinations.

Concrete experiment ideas (ranked by effort):
1) KV compaction replay (effort: low-medium):
   - take a week of live traffic traces (anonymized) from staging and snapshot kv-access patterns.
   - implement offline compressor that keeps 1:1 for last 1024 tokens and compresses older tokens using PCA-like projection to 256-dim.
   - replay on a lightweight evaluator (50 queries) drawn from our eval set; measure LM perplexity change, retrieval-hit rate for long-range context references, and per-request token delta.
   - success signal: <2% quality drop, >25% effective KV memory reduction.

2) Two-tier batching proxy (effort: medium):
   - add routing flag in the proxy for "latency-critical" that bypasses the jumbo batcher and goes to a small-window greedy batcher.
   - route 5% of staging traffic as latency-critical and capture 1) p50/p95/p99 latency, 2) tokens/server, 3) cost-per-request.
   - offline simulation first: feed batcher with mixed arrival patterns to tune window size.

3) Prompt robustness vs quantization (effort: low):
   - pick 40 prompts from product features (chat completion, code generation, summarization).
   - run each prompt through fp16, int8, and 4-bit variants (same model family) and compute: answer divergence metric (token-level edit distance), and annotate 20 outputs for hallucination severity.
   - if divergence concentrated on punctuation or formatting, test a lightweight prompt normalizer.

4) Canary policy: model fallback policy test (effort: low):
   - configure a canary route that falls back from a high-capacity low-cost quantized model to a higher-precision model on hallucination signals (heuristic: factuality score drop).
   - simulate with crafted prompts that trigger hallucination to ensure fallback happens and measure user-facing latency.

Operational checks to add to the console (short list):
- KV memory heatmap by route: show distribution of kv footprint across requests (helps triage spike sources).
- Per-route quantization delta: small dashboard showing quality delta between baseline and quantized variant (sampled prompts and human/auto metrics).
- Fast-path utilization metric: % of requests that qualify and % served on fast-path vs queued.

Notes from last week’s workshop (mini takeaways):
- SREs emphasised observability of queueing delays inside the batcher — we often track only total request latency, not time spent waiting in batch window. Need histograms for queue time.
- Solutions folks recommended a "budgeted recall" pattern for RAG: keep first-pass retrieval cheap and cache richer context only for long-lived sessions.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How effective is offline KV compaction vs on-the-fly incremental compaction? Does compaction introduce artifact tokens that cause degradation?
- For two-tier batching: what percentage of traffic is latency-sensitive across product routes? We need sampling.
- How to automatically detect meaningful hallucination signals cheaply in prod for canary fallback without human labels?

Immediate next steps (this week):
- Run the prompt robustness vs quantization experiment on a small sample set (Iris help requested). Expected runtime: <1 day on dev cluster.
- Ask SRE to add queue-time histogram to the batcher metrics (file JIRA-ENG-1298).
- Draft quick design doc for KV compaction replay and share with Noah for review.

Things to capture later (backlog):
- Small UX experiment: expose "precision preference" toggle in console for devs to target cost vs quality per-route.
- Policy ideas for multi-variant fallbacks (region-aware routing + model variant fallback chain).

Random micro-notes (for memory):
- Remember to scrub user ids from traffic snapshot; use hashed IDs.
- Check existing kernel selection logs: see if there are persistent kernels that dominate for long sequences (possible warm-start opportunity).

References I should re-read:
- blog: "quantization prompt strategies" (link saved in channel #devex-readings)
- paper: "adaptive batching under tight SLAs" (ICLR talk notes PDF)
- internal: kv-cache-primer Confluence page (linked above)

If I get time today: spin up quick FP16 vs Int8 run for 10 prompts and paste results below (will append).

-- Felicity
